answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This seven-line poem is entirely Dickinson's own work. It went unpublished in her lifetime and first appeared four years after her death in Poems (1890) ↗, the collection edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson — confirmed by reading the poem's text in that edition.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Poems by Emily Dickinson — “Life,” No. VI
Mabel Loomis Todd & Thomas Wentworth Higginson

source.excerpt:
If I can stop one heart from breaking,
I shall not live in vain;
If I can ease one life the aching,
Or cool one pain,
Or help one fainting robin
Unto his nest again,
I shall not live in vain.
trail: First printed posthumously in 1890, as poem VI of the “Life” section in Poems ↗, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson.
The same wording is preserved at Wikisource ↗, transcribed from that 1890 edition.
A later printing survives in full scan at the Internet Archive ↗ (1893 Roberts Brothers printing of the same Todd & Higginson collection).
Reprinted again in Martha Dickinson Bianchi's 1924 Complete Poems of Emily Dickinson, as cited on Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1890 first edition regularized Dickinson's characteristic dashes into standard commas and semicolons, as was common editorial practice of the era — the words themselves are hers.

author.name: Emily Dickinson
author.heading: About Emily Dickinson
author.bio: Emily Dickinson spent most of her life in seclusion in Amherst, Massachusetts, writing nearly 1,800 poems while publishing fewer than a dozen in her lifetime. Her sister Lavinia discovered the manuscripts after her death in 1886, and editors began publishing them — starting with this poem, in 1890.

context.heading: A rare moment of Dickinson without a riddle
lead: Most of Dickinson's nearly 1,800 poems are famous for their compression, dashes, and slant rhyme — puzzles as much as statements. This one is unusual for stating its thesis almost plainly: a single act of kindness, stopping one heart from breaking or helping one fainting bird home, is reason enough to have lived.

She never published it. Like almost everything she wrote, it stayed in manuscript until her sister Lavinia found nearly two thousand poems after Dickinson's death in 1886 and pushed to get them into print, resulting in the heavily-edited 1890 Poems.
